evals.prompt: I have the diamonds dataset at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/diamonds.parquet (3,000 rows, 11 columns). I'm about to fit a regression to predict price, but first I want a holistic distribution check on all the variables — what's numeric, what's categorical, are there any data-quality issues. Walk me through it.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py to load the parquet, finds and reads diamonds_description.md to learn the column meanings (price in dollars, carat is weight, cut/color/clarity are graded categoricals, x/y/z are physical dimensions in mm, depth/table are angles, date is the observation date). Fits with rsm.eda.distr(df, name='diamonds') and calls .summary() — prints the holistic per-column summary. Walks through: header (11 columns: 7 numeric, 3 categorical, 1 other) and flags this as the first sanity check. NUMERIC: explicitly compares mean vs median for each numeric column. Calls out price as heavily right-skewed (mean ≈ $3,907 vs median ≈ $2,407, a >60% gap) — recommends considering a log transform for price before regression. Calls out carat as mildly right-skewed. Notes the physical-dimension variables (x, y, z, depth, table) are roughly symmetric. CATEGORICAL: walks through each (clarity 8 levels, cut 5 levels, color 7 levels), notes that all categoricals have well-populated levels (smallest is clarity I1 with 40 obs, ~1.3%) — no tiny-level issues to collapse. Flags the data quality summary: no missingness, all categoricals usable, price/carat skew is the main modeling consideration. OTHER: notes that the date column spans 2012-02-26 to 2015-12-01 (~4 years, 30 distinct dates suggesting monthly snapshots). Recommends running d.plot() to visualize the distributions (would compose 10 plots — 7 histograms + 3 bar charts in a 2-column grid).

evals.prompt: Same diamonds data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/diamonds.parquet. Now I want to (a) run d.plot() and visualize, but specifically I want the price histogram on a LOG x-axis since you flagged the skew, and (b) compare the histogram of price and log(price) side by side so I can see the effect of the transform. Walk me through the plotnine layering.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: explicitly demonstrates the plotnine extensibility of distr.plot(). (1) Calls rsm.eda.distr(df) and stores result as `d`. (2) Builds the single-column price plot p = d.plot(cols=['price']), then layers a log x-scale and a title: p + scale_x_log10() + labs(title='Diamond Prices (log scale)') — explicitly explains that d.plot() returns a plotnine.ggplot object that supports any plotnine addition. (3) For the before/after comparison, RECOMMENDS the polars-then-distr workflow: first transform the data with d.data.with_columns(price_log=pl.col('price').log()), then re-run distr on the transformed DataFrame: rsm.eda.distr(transformed, cols=['price', 'price_log']).plot() — this produces a 2-panel grid showing the linear price (right-skewed) and the log-transformed price (much more symmetric, approximately bell-shaped) side by side. Names the pattern: 'distr.plot() is the START of the plotnine pipeline, not the end — you can add any plotnine layer (scale, theme, geom_vline for reference lines, facet_wrap, etc.) on top.' Optionally mentions even further extensions: layering a vertical line at the mean and median with geom_vline, using a different theme with theme_minimal(), saving to file with p.save('plot.png', width=12, height=8). Re-confirms that this is the canonical pyrsm.eda 'extend with plotnine' pattern that the user can apply to any plotnine-returning eda function.

Conversation that: notices the path is not absolute (uses ~), asks the user for the absolute path before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tilde or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I ran rsm.eda.distr on a dataset that has a column 'rating' which is integer 1-5. distr classified it as categorical, but I want it as numeric so I can compute mean rating. The data is at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/diamonds.parquet — but I'm using a synthetic column. Actually let me ask the general question: how does distr decide categorical vs numeric, and how do I override it?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) explains the classification heuristic clearly: distr classifies a column as CATEGORICAL if (a) the dtype is String/Utf8/Categorical/Enum, OR (b) the dtype is an integer type AND n_unique < `nint` (default 25). Otherwise it's classified as NUMERIC (for float dtypes always; for integer dtypes when n_unique >= nint). (2) Explains the design motivation: a 1-5 integer rating is 'really' an ordinal categorical — computing its mean (e.g., 3.2) is occasionally meaningful but the modal level and the frequency table are usually MORE informative. The default nint=25 is generous because it captures rating scales, low-cardinality survey responses, etc. without false positives. (3) Gives the user TWO override mechanisms: (a) lower `nint` to force more integer columns to numeric — e.g., rsm.eda.distr(df, nint=0) treats all integer columns as numeric regardless of n_unique; (b) pre-cast the column with df.with_columns(pl.col('rating').cast(pl.Float64)) — float dtype is always numeric in distr's classification. (4) Walks through a concrete example: if `rating` is Int8 with values 1-5 (n_unique=5 < 25), default distr classifies it categorical → frequency table. With nint=0 or after casting to Float, distr classifies it numeric → mean/median/min/max/sd. (5) Mentions that BOTH views are often useful and you can ask distr to show both by calling it twice on the same DataFrame with different nint settings or by manually using pyrsm.eda.explore on just the rating column to get its mean. (6) Optionally cautions: 'mean rating' is statistically valid for an ordinal scale but is sometimes criticized; the median or the modal response are often more defensible summaries — the choice depends on the question being asked.
